title: Your neighbor
hook: faith lived beside neighbors of every kind

segments.voice: Yesterday, your family. Your line: pray together. Did you do one chore before anyone asked? Home has walls. On the other side of one of them, somebody else lives. Today, that person. Day one thousand four hundred nine.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once told his companions something surprising about the angel Jibril. Jibril, he said, kept urging me to treat the neighbor well, so often that I thought he was going to make the neighbor an heir. That report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. An heir. Someone with a share in what is yours, written into the family accounts. The person whose music comes through the wall, whose car blocks yours, whose name you might not even know. Today, faith lived beside neighbors of every kind.
screen: `JIBRIL KEPT URGING.` → `AS IF THE NEIGHBOR WERE AN HEIR.` → `THE ONE THROUGH THE WALL.`

segments.voice: Start with the Qur'an. In surah an-Nisa, in a list of those to be treated with kindness, after parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, it names the neighbor who is related to you, the neighbor who is a stranger, and the companion at your side. Two kinds of neighbor, side by side in one verse: the one who shares your family and the one who shares nothing with you but a fence. Next, how high the bar is set. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his neighbor. And in the same collection, he says that a person whose neighbor is not safe from his harm will not enter paradise. So a neighbor is not a matter of manners. It sits right next to faith itself. Third, neighbors of every kind. A report in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi tells of the companion Abdullah ibn Amr, who had a sheep slaughtered at home and asked his household: have you given some to our Jewish neighbor? He then repeated the hadith of Jibril and the neighbor. The neighbor's faith did not change the neighbor's right. Last, what this asks on an ordinary street. It doesn't start with big gestures. It starts with knowing a name. Not letting your trash cans block a driveway. Keeping the noise down at night. A plate of food over the fence on a holiday, any holiday. Checking on the older man upstairs when it snows. Rights like these are small, and they are owed whether or not the neighbor returns them.
screen: `THE NEAR NEIGHBOR AND THE STRANGER.` · `HONOR YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `HAVE YOU GIVEN SOME NEXT DOOR?` · `SMALL RIGHTS, OWED ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: meet a neighbor. To begin, sit and let your breath slow. In your mind, step out your front door. Look left. Look right. Look up or down, if you live in a building. Name, silently, every neighbor whose name you know. Notice where the names run out. Pick one door where you don't know a name, or where you know a name and nothing else. Let one small, easy reason to knock come to mind: an introduction, a plate of something, a question about the building. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless the people on your street. After the bell, if it's a sensible hour, knock, or leave a short note. The bell holds the time.
Your neighbor. The person on the other side of the wall, whose rights the Qur'an and the Prophet set right next to faith. Today's word.
Your line: start next door. Today, learn one neighbor's name, or use the name you already know when you say hello. Tomorrow, your service. Day one thousand four hundred nine.

howItsDone: Muslims treat the neighbor's rights as part of faith, following the Qur'an's command to be kind to the near and the stranger neighbor and the hadith 'let him honor his neighbor'; this can mean sharing food on holidays, avoiding noise and harm, and checking on neighbors of any faith.

options: have you given some to our Jewish neighbor?
have you kept enough for us?

fork.reveal: he asked whether they had given some to their Jewish neighbor, and repeated the Prophet's words about Jibril urging care for the neighbor (Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi).

trapdoor: what you thought: a neighbor is whoever happens to live nearby.
what it means: someone with real rights over you, whatever their faith, starting with a name, a plate of food and no harm.
what a scholar hears: an-Nisa's near neighbor and stranger neighbor, Jibril urging until the neighbor seemed an heir, and Abdullah ibn Amr's question about his Jewish neighbor.

notes: Confirm Sahih al-Bukhari 6014 (Jibril and the neighbor as heir), Sahih Muslim 47 (let him honor his neighbor) and Sahih Muslim 46 (whose neighbor is not safe from his harm).
Qur'an 4:36 is paraphrased; check the rendering of 'the neighbor who is related', 'the neighbor who is a stranger' and 'the companion at your side'.
Check the Abdullah ibn Amr report (Abu Dawud 5152; Tirmidhi 1943), its grading.
The everyday examples (trash cans, noise, food on a holiday, checking on an older neighbor) are illustrations, not sourced rulings.

Editor: 'let him honor his neighbor' moved from Sahih al-Bukhari 6018 (whose wording there is 'let him not harm his neighbor', and which day 1393 already used) to Sahih Muslim 47, where 'honor his neighbor' is the wording.
